### The scaling

**Point sources · background-dominated limit**

$$
N_s\propto\mathcal E,\qquad
N_b\propto\mathcal E\,\sigma_\theta^2,
\qquad Z\simeq\frac{N_s}{\sqrt{N_b}}
\propto\frac{\sqrt{\mathcal E}}{\sigma_\theta}
$$

| Change | Signal | Background | Significance |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $4\times$ exposure | $4\times$ | $4\times$ | $2\times$ |
| $2\times$ sharper directions | unchanged | $\div4$ | $2\times$ |
| Both | $4\times$ | unchanged | $4\times$ |

Calibration controls pointing and energy systematics.

A global network adds sky coverage and rapid follow-up.

::: {.media-caption}
Idealized scaling, fixed spectrum and event selection.
[Gen2 science case](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.04323) ·
[Upgrade calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.09441)

::: {.notes}
**Say:** A source does not appear at once: neutrinos trickle in, most of them background, and the source only stands out when its excess beats the noise — so we win either by collecting longer and with bigger detectors, or by pointing more sharply.

The film (about 57 s, English): events arrive one by one on a 10-degree patch;
the count in a circle around the source is compared with the expected background
and the significance grows as the square root of time. Then the same source and
years are shown for cascades in ice (half of the events within 10 degrees),
cascades in water (2.5 degrees) and tracks (0.4 degrees): about 0.3, 1.1 and 6
sigma expected after 1 km³ × 10 years. Finally cascades in water in 1 and 30 km³:
1.1 versus 5.9 sigma expected (this simulated sky: 1.0 and 5.6). The source
strength is of the order of the 79 (+22/−20) NGC 1068 events in IceCube over
2011–2020 (Science 378 (2022) 538); the background is uniform and identical in all
panels, an idealisation (real tracks and cascades differ in background and
effective area). Significance: Poisson likelihood ratio at the known position,
expectation from the Asimov data set; maps show the same statistic around every
pixel, so 2–3 sigma noise blobs elsewhere are expected. Angular scales: IceCube
2013 cascades 10–15 degrees; Baikal-GVD cascades above 200 TeV r50 = 1.6–3.3
degrees (ApJ 982 (2025) 73, Table 1); tracks ≤ 0.4 degrees (Ahlers and Halzen
2018). It is not a forecast for Baikal-GVD, IceCube-Gen2, KM3NeT or B-HUNT.
Film source and provenance: `media/sensitivity/SOURCES.md`.

Spend about 90 seconds before the observatory overview. Mathcal E is a relative
exposure scale, not neutrino energy. At fixed detector response,
it can mean observation time; a scalar acceptance increase is an alternative
only if it scales signal and background rates alike. N_s and N_b are expected
counts, and sigma_theta denotes a characteristic small-angle point-spread width.
For a window whose radius scales with sigma_theta, its solid angle scales as
sigma_theta squared. The contained signal fraction stays fixed as the window
shrinks with the improved resolution; locally uniform background decreases
with the window area. Z is the Gaussian, large-background counting approximation,
not a calibrated significance from a real telescope's likelihood analysis.

The table compares factors at fixed incident source flux, spectrum, energy
range and selection. Four times the exposure yields four times each count
and twice the approximate significance. Halving the angular width retains
the same signal fraction and divides the background by four, again doubling Z.
Combining the two changes leaves background equal to baseline and gives four
times the signal and significance. The arithmetic is a scaling illustration,
not a forecast for Gen2, GVD, ARCA or any named detector.

The approximation fails for sparse/background-free samples, large angles,
extended sources, response changes and dominant systematics. Trials and
time/energy information are absent. The minimum detectable flux scales as
sigma_theta / sqrt(E) in this idealized limit, so both gains improve it.

Calibration constrains optical-medium, timing, charge and geometry uncertainties.
More exposure does not remove these systematic errors. Different latitudes
add complementary coverage; alerts enable time-dependent counterpart searches.
Do not treat exposures of different telescopes as interchangeable without
their energy- and direction-dependent responses.

Use the scaling to read the instrument designs that follow: exposure, angular
information and control of systematics serve different scientific purposes.

References: IceCube-Gen2 science case, https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.04323;
IceCube Upgrade design and calibration goals,
https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.09441. The displayed factors follow analytically
from the stated counting model, rather than from a collaboration forecast.
:::
